Process introspection is being filtered: Process introspection is being filtered by the kernel (typical EDR / Windows 24H2 hardening). A kernel-level filter (typically EDR --: A kernel-level filter (typically EDR -- CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Defender ATP, etc.) is blocking process introspection. Endpoint-protection software is present. If the daemon is crashing with NTSTATUS codes, these products may be the cause.

The daemon started and is listening, but: The daemon started and is listening, but loopback connections to it are blocked. Open 127.0.0.1 traffic in the host firewall / endpoint-protection product.
A system policy (AppLocker / SRP / Windo: A system policy (AppLocker / SRP / Windows Defender Application Control) blocked the daemon from running. IT must add an allow rule.
The daemon port is held by a process Fac: The daemon port is held by a process Factory cannot terminate (typically an EDR-protected service). Reboot to clear the port.
TLS verification failed -- a corporate M: TLS verification failed -- a corporate MITM proxy is likely intercepting HTTPS. The proxy CA must be trusted for Factory to authenticate. Allow-list api.factory.ai or install the proxy root certificate in the system trust store.
Could not reach api.factory.ai over TLS. Check firewall rules and proxy configuration.

Factory could not start because another: Factory could not start because another application is bound to its port. Quit that app or reboot.
Port is held by a dead process (zombie s: Port is held by a dead process (zombie socket). The Windows kernel TCP endpoint table is stale -- typically caused by an endpoint-protection kernel driver holding a socket handle reference. A reboot is required.
An EDR-protected process holds the daemo: An EDR-protected process holds the daemon port and cannot be terminated by user-level Factory. Reboot or have IT free port {{port}}.
PID {{pid}} owns port {{port}} but is no: PID {{pid}} owns port {{port}} but is not responding as a Factory daemon. The original daemon process likely exited and the OS recycled this PID. A reboot may be required, or the process holding the port needs to be terminated.
The Windows kernel reports PID {{pid}} a: The Windows kernel reports PID {{pid}} as owning port {{port}} in LISTEN state, but that process no longer exists. This is an orphaned kernel socket entry -- typically caused by an endpoint-protection kernel driver (WFP/TDI filter) holding a socket handle reference after the process exited. A reboot is required to clear it. Run "netstat -ano | findstr {{port}}" in an admin terminal to confirm.
